title: The Three Components of Angular Momentum Cannot be Measured Simultaneously with Arbitrary Precision
lead: The orbital angular momentum of a particle has three components, and quantum mechanics turns each into an operator. Whether two of them can be measured at once depends on whether their operators commute.
objectives: Understand how to measure the orbital angular momentum of an electron around a nucleus.
Understand how the Heisenburgh Uncertainty Principle extends to orbital angular momenta.
Manipulate the angular momenta cyclic permutations that allow two of the three projects to be simultaneous measured
summary_html:
In the quantum world, angular momentum is quantized. The square of the magnitude of the angular momentum (determined by the eigenvalues of the $\hat{L^2}$ operator) can only assume one of the discrete set of values

$$ L^2 = l(l + 1)\hbar^2 $$

or the magnitude of the angular momentum

$$ L = \sqrt{l(l + 1)}\hbar $$

with $l = 0, 1, 2, ...$

The z-component of the angular momentum (i.e., projection of $L$ onto the $z$-axis) is also quantized with

$$ L_z= m_{l} \hbar $$

with $m_l = -l, 0-1, ..., 0, ... +l +1, l$ for a given value of $l$. Hence, $l$ and $m_l$ are the angular momentum quantum number and the magnetic quantum number, respectively.
notes: Adapted from Richard Fitzpatrick (The University of Texas at Austin) under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with Figure 6.3.1 by Maschen in the public domain.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise in this section. All three exercises, on the l = 2 vector model, the commutator of the y and z components and the z component acting on the l = 1 spherical harmonics, were written by AI with AI solutions; their Bloom levels and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

exercises.prompt: An electron in a hydrogen atom has $l = 2$. Draw its vector model as in Figure 6.3.1. (a) What is the magnitude $|\kLvec|$ of its angular momentum, in units of $\hbar$? What angle does the vector make with the z axis (b) when $m_l = +2$ and (c) when $m_l = +1$? Give the angles in degrees.

parts.hint: The vector's z component is $m_l\hbar$, so $\cos\theta = m_l/\sqrt{l(l+1)}$.

answer.solution: By Equation 6.3.8, $|\kLvec| = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\,\hbar = \sqrt{6}\,\hbar = 2.449\,\hbar$. The z component can be $m_l\hbar$ with $m_l = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2$ (Equation 6.3.9), so the vector model has five cones. The angle $\theta$ to the z axis has $\cos\theta = \kLz/|\kLvec| = m_l/\sqrt{6}$. For $m_l = +2$, $\cos\theta = 2/2.449 = 0.8165$ and $\theta = 35.26°$. For $m_l = +1$, $\cos\theta = 0.4082$ and $\theta = 65.91°$. Since $|m_l| < \sqrt{l(l+1)}$ for every allowed $m_l$, the angle is never zero: the vector never points along the z axis.

exercises.prompt: Use the fundamental commutation relations of the position and momentum operators, as was done for $[\kLxhat, \kLyhat]$, to show that $[\kLyhat, \kLzhat] = {\rm i}\hbar\kLxhat$ (Equation 6.3.11).

answer.hint: Expand $[\kz\kpx - \kx\kpz, \kx\kpy - \ky\kpx]$ into four commutators and keep the ones where a coordinate meets its own momentum.
answer.solution:
With $\kLyhat = \kz\kpx - \kx\kpz$ and $\kLzhat = \kx\kpy - \ky\kpx$,

$$ [\kLyhat, \kLzhat] = [\kz\kpx, \kx\kpy] - [\kz\kpx, \ky\kpx] - [\kx\kpz, \kx\kpy] + [\kx\kpz, \ky\kpx] $$

In the second and third commutators no coordinate meets its own momentum, so both are zero. In the first only $\kpx$ and $\kx$ fail to commute, so $[\kz\kpx, \kx\kpy] = \kz\kpy[\kpx, \kx] = -{\rm i}\hbar\,\kz\kpy$. In the fourth only $\kx$ and $\kpx$ fail to commute, so $[\kx\kpz, \ky\kpx] = \ky\kpz[\kx, \kpx] = {\rm i}\hbar\,\ky\kpz$. Adding,

$$ [\kLyhat, \kLzhat] = {\rm i}\hbar\,(\ky\kpz - \kz\kpy) = {\rm i}\hbar\,\kLxhat $$

exercises.prompt: The spherical harmonics with $l = 1$ are $Y_1^{0} = \left(\dfrac{3}{4\pi}\right)^{1/2}\cos\theta$ and $Y_1^{\pm 1} = \mp\left(\dfrac{3}{8\pi}\right)^{1/2}\sin\theta\, e^{\pm {\rm i}\kvarphi}$. Let $\kLzhat = -{\rm i}\hbar\,\partial/\partial\kvarphi$ act on each. What eigenvalue, in units of $\hbar$, does it give for (a) $Y_1^{+1}$, (b) $Y_1^{0}$ and (c) $Y_1^{-1}$?

parts.hint: The derivative of $e^{{\rm i}\kvarphi}$ with respect to $\kvarphi$ is ${\rm i}e^{{\rm i}\kvarphi}$.

answer.solution: Only the factor $e^{\pm{\rm i}\kvarphi}$ depends on $\kvarphi$. For $Y_1^{+1}$, $\partial Y_1^{+1}/\partial\kvarphi = {\rm i}\,Y_1^{+1}$, so $\kLzhat Y_1^{+1} = -{\rm i}\hbar({\rm i})Y_1^{+1} = +\hbar\, Y_1^{+1}$. $Y_1^{0}$ holds no $\kvarphi$, so $\kLzhat Y_1^{0} = 0$. For $Y_1^{-1}$ the derivative brings down $-{\rm i}$, so $\kLzhat Y_1^{-1} = -\hbar\, Y_1^{-1}$. The eigenvalues are $m_l\hbar$ with $m_l = +1, 0, -1$, as Equation 6.3.9 says.

footnotes.html: The magnitude is meant: Equation 6.3.8 gives the length of $\vec{L}$, as the Summary says.
The operator is $\hat{L}_z$ and its eigenvalue is $m_l\hbar$, with the $m_l$ of the next line: $\hat{L}_z Y_l^{m_l} = m_l\hbar\, Y_l^{m_l}$.
The commutator worked next is that of $\hat{L}_x$ and $\hat{L}_y$.
Solving one problem gives the shared eigenfunctions $|\psi\rangle$, not the eigenvalues; each operator still has its own eigenvalues.

derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 6.3 The Three Components of Angular Momentum Cannot be Measured Simultaneously with Arbitrary Precision

assumes.text: The chain rule: a derivative with respect to $\kvarphi$ at fixed $\kr$ and $\ktheta$ is $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\kvarphi} = \dfrac{\partial\kx}{\partial\kvarphi}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\kx} + \dfrac{\partial\ky}{\partial\kvarphi}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\ky} + \dfrac{\partial\kz}{\partial\kvarphi}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\kz}$.

steps.cap: Only $\kvarphi$ changes, so $\kr$ and $\ktheta$ are constants: the derivative of $\cos\kvarphi$ is $-\sin\kvarphi$, that of $\sin\kvarphi$ is $\cos\kvarphi$, and $\kz$ holds no $\kvarphi$ at all.

derivations.what: the commutator of the x and y components
derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 6.3 The Three Components of Angular Momentum Cannot be Measured Simultaneously with Arbitrary Precision

assumes.text: A commutator is linear in each of its two places: $[\kAhat - \kBhat, \hat{C} - \hat{D}] = [\kAhat, \hat{C}] - [\kAhat, \hat{D}] - [\kBhat, \hat{C}] + [\kBhat, \hat{D}]$.

then.why: The operators are written from the classical components, as the section assumes.

steps.cap: Only a coordinate and its own momentum fail to commute, and no such pair meets in $[\ky\,\kpz, \kx\,\kpz]$ or in $[\kz\,\kpy, \kz\,\kpx]$, so both vanish.
In the first commutator only $\kpz$ and $\kz$ fail to commute, so $\ky$ and $\kpx$ come outside it; in the second, $\kx$ and $\kpy$ do.
$[\kz, \kpz] = {\rm i}\hbar$, and swapping the two places of a commutator changes its sign, so $[\kpz, \kz] = -{\rm i}\hbar$.

nodes.note: The book introduces this work as the commutator of $\hat{L}_x$ and $\hat{L}_z$; it computes that of $\hat{L}_x$ and $\hat{L}_y$.

derivations.what: the square of the angular momentum commutes with its x component
derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 6.3 The Three Components of Angular Momentum Cannot be Measured Simultaneously with Arbitrary Precision, Example 6.3.1

assumes.text: A commutator is linear in each place: $[\kAhat + \kBhat, \hat{C}] = [\kAhat, \hat{C}] + [\kBhat, \hat{C}]$.
For a square, $[\kAhat^2, \kBhat] = \kAhat[\kAhat, \kBhat] + [\kAhat, \kBhat]\kAhat$, since both sides expand to $\kAhat\kAhat\kBhat - \kBhat\kAhat\kAhat$.

steps.cap: $\kLxhat^2\kLxhat$ and $\kLxhat\kLxhat^2$ are both $\kLxhat\kLxhat\kLxhat$, so their difference is zero.
The first two terms and the final two terms can be rewritten as different commutators, by the rule for a square.
Swapping the two places of a commutator changes its sign, so $[\kLyhat, \kLxhat] = -{\rm i}\hbar\kLzhat$.

nodes.note: The book writes the first of the related forms as $[\hat{L}_y, \hat{L}_x] = \hat{L}_y + \hat{L}_y[\hat{L}_y, \hat{L}_x]$, which is meant as $[\hat{L}_y, \hat{L}_x]\hat{L}_y + \hat{L}_y[\hat{L}_y, \hat{L}_x]$; it also writes $Lz$ for $\hat{L}_z$ and $ih$ for ${\rm i}\hbar$ in the last lines.
